---
title: "Units of assignment"
---

Suppose an experiment compares word recognition after familiar accent training and unfamiliar accent training. Each participant completes 40 recognition trials, so a study with 24 participants produces 960 rows. What receives the training condition?

The answer is the participant, not the trial. Training happens once, before any of the 40 responses are collected. The [**unit of assignment**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics) is the entity that can independently receive a condition. Identifying this unit is the first step in reconstructing what was randomized and how many independent assignments the study contains.

## Assignment and observation are different maps

Let $r$ index rows in the recorded table. Each row belongs to an assignment unit $g(r)$, and that unit receives condition $Z_{g(r)}$. The condition attached to row $r$ is thus

$$
Z_r=Z_{g(r)}.
$$

When the participant is the unit of assignment, every row from the same participant has the same value of $g(r)$ and the same assigned condition. If there are $N=960$ rows but $G=24$ participants, then there are 24 independent assignments, not 960. The rows remain useful because they measure each participant repeatedly. But they do not multiply the number of times training was assigned.

The [**unit of observation**](https://bookdown.org/pkaldunn/Book/UnitsObsAnalysis.html) answers a different question. It is the entity represented by one measured response, such as a word recognition trial. The [unit of analysis](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd) describes the entities compared by a particular statistical calculation. These three units can coincide, but they need not.

## Working through a small study

Consider four participants, each of whom responds to three words.

| participant | training | word | correct |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|
| P1 | familiar | w1 | 1 |
| P1 | familiar | w2 | 1 |
| P1 | familiar | w3 | 0 |
| P2 | unfamiliar | w1 | 0 |
| P2 | unfamiliar | w2 | 1 |
| P2 | unfamiliar | w3 | 0 |
| P3 | familiar | w1 | 1 |
| P3 | familiar | w2 | 1 |
| P3 | familiar | w3 | 1 |
| P4 | unfamiliar | w1 | 1 |
| P4 | unfamiliar | w2 | 0 |
| P4 | unfamiliar | w3 | 0 |

There are 12 observations because 12 recognition responses were recorded. There are only four assignment units because the training condition could vary independently only across participants. The assignment counts are two familiar and two unfamiliar participants.

We can recover both counts from the table.

```{r}
trials <- data.frame(
  participant = rep(paste0("P", 1:4), each = 3),
  training = rep(c("familiar", "unfamiliar", "familiar", "unfamiliar"), each = 3),
  word = rep(paste0("w", 1:3), times = 4),
  correct = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)
)

nrow(trials)
participant_assignment <- unique(trials[c("participant", "training")])
nrow(participant_assignment)
table(participant_assignment$training)
```

The call to `unique()` implements the definition above. It retains one row for each distinct assignment unit and its condition. A design audit should perform this reduction before counting assignments.

## Asking what could have varied independently

The most reliable diagnostic is counterfactual and procedural: under the actual assignment procedure, what could have received a different condition? In the training study, one trial could not switch training while the other trials from the same participant remained unchanged. The participant is thus the assignment unit.

The same question applies at other levels. If an instructional intervention is assigned by classroom and responses are collected from individual students, the classroom is the unit of assignment. If an acoustic manipulation is applied once to an entire block, the block receives that manipulation. And if an item version is independently chosen for each presentation, the presentation may be the assignment unit, subject to any participant and item constraints.

## Response rows do not count assignments

Treating the unit represented by a row as an independent assignment unit would count 960 assignments rather than 24. The resulting uncertainty would appear too small because responses sharing one assignment are treated as if training had been assigned repeatedly. This is the same dependence problem developed for [repeated linguistic observations](../regression-models/structured-data.qmd), now stated in terms of the assignment procedure.

The number of response rows does not change the number of independent condition assignments. A model may represent the fact that responses share participants, but it cannot create assignment variation that the experiment did not produce.

## Writing the design in three sentences

Before collection, write one sentence for each unit.

1. One row of the raw data represents one word recognition trial.
2. Training condition is assigned once to each participant.
3. Responses are repeated within participants and words.

This compact description exposes the design before model notation obscures it. It also records which repeated units the earlier [mixed effects models](../regression-models/structured-data.qmd) must preserve when they are applied to this study.

::: {.callout-note title="Audit the assignment unit"}
1. A classroom receives a teaching method, and each student supplies five responses. What is the assignment unit, and what is the observation unit?
2. A participant hears 60 words, with accent independently selected for each word subject to equal condition counts. What could receive a different condition under the procedure?
3. Why can additional trials improve measurement without adding independent assignments?
:::

The unit of assignment is the entity whose condition could vary independently under the actual design. Separating it from the row of the data fixes the level at which assignment must operate.
